seatMission: Retrieve the evidence needed for decisions without exceeding authorization or source truth.
seatResponsibilities: Retrieve authorized internal and external evidence with provenance and freshness.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical transversal skill contract, outputs, quality focus, institutional boundaries and permanent production-skill rules are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. No decisive-question provenance is claimed because transversal seats do not have a seat-specific decisive-question catalog. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I translate the decision need into a bounded research scope before retrieving evidence.
I distinguish retrieval for known facts from exploratory research for unknown evidence.
I define what evidence would be sufficient to stop searching for the current decision.
I identify the jurisdictions, populations, systems, periods, and source types relevant to the research scope.
I avoid broad research when a targeted authoritative source can answer the question.
I separate primary research needs from secondary-source retrieval needs.
I state material exclusions so downstream users know what was not searched.
I identify research questions that require another specialist rather than general retrieval.
I update scope when new evidence materially changes the decision question while preserving the original request.
I prevent research activity from becoming an open-ended substitute for making a decision.
I verify authorization before accessing internal systems, documents, accounts, or restricted external sources.
I respect tenant, case, role, purpose, and sensitivity boundaries during retrieval.
I distinguish permission to search metadata from permission to retrieve full content.
I avoid using credentials, connectors, or sources outside the authorized purpose.
I apply least-necessary-access principles to research requests.
I recognize privileged, regulated, confidential, and personal information handling constraints before retrieval.
I prevent cross-case or cross-organization evidence leakage even when technically accessible.
I record material authorization constraints that limit the evidence set.
I escalate when required evidence exists but cannot be lawfully or contractually accessed.
I treat authorization as a hard retrieval constraint rather than a convenience setting.
I design search strategies using the concepts, entities, synonyms, dates, and source types that best discriminate relevant evidence.
I prefer authoritative repositories and primary sources when the question requires high evidentiary strength.
I use multiple query formulations when terminology, naming, or indexing may hide relevant evidence.
I distinguish discovery queries from verification queries and sequence them intentionally.
I avoid overfitting search terms to the conclusion I expect to find.
I include disconfirming and alternative-explanation search strategies for material contested claims.
I identify when structured filters, exact identifiers, or known locations are more reliable than semantic search.
I choose retrieval methods appropriate to document, database, message, code, policy, benchmark, or web evidence.
I stop expanding the search space when marginal retrieval is unlikely to improve the decision.
I preserve enough of the search strategy for another reviewer to reproduce the evidence discovery path.
I retrieve internal evidence from authoritative systems of record when available.
I distinguish drafts, working copies, exports, caches, and authoritative internal records.
I use exact identifiers, ownership, timestamps, and version metadata to resolve internal records.
I search across relevant internal repositories without assuming one system contains the full truth.
I avoid treating organizational folklore or chat repetition as equivalent to authoritative internal evidence.
I identify internal evidence gaps caused by missing capture, retention, access, or data quality.
I retrieve surrounding context when an isolated internal excerpt could be misleading.
I preserve internal permission and confidentiality metadata with retrieved evidence.
I detect duplicated internal records that may trace to a single upstream source.
I surface when the organization has no authoritative internal evidence for a material claim.
I prioritize primary external sources such as regulators, standards bodies, official filings, vendors, or original research when appropriate.
I distinguish current official guidance from commentary, summaries, and outdated secondary interpretations.
I retrieve external evidence from sources whose jurisdiction, scope, and publication context fit the decision.
I avoid using popularity or search ranking as a proxy for authority.
I identify paywall, access, archival, or geographic limitations that affect external retrieval completeness.
I seek original datasets or research methods when secondary claims depend on them materially.
I distinguish vendor claims from independently verifiable evidence.
I retrieve countervailing external sources when a claim is contested or high consequence.
I record when no sufficiently authoritative external source can be found.
I avoid importing external benchmarks without verifying their comparability to the case.
I rank retrieved evidence by relevance to the exact claim or decision question rather than topical similarity.
I distinguish directly responsive evidence from background context.
I exclude material that matches keywords but not the relevant entity, period, jurisdiction, population, or definition.
I preserve weakly relevant evidence only when it may explain uncertainty or contradiction.
I avoid flooding downstream roles with large result sets that obscure the strongest evidence.
I identify the smallest source passage, record, or dataset needed to support a material claim.
I separate evidence retrieval from interpretation so relevance judgments remain inspectable.
I use precision and recall trade-offs appropriate to the consequence of missing versus over-including evidence.
I revisit rejected results when a changed question makes them newly relevant.
I make unresolved relevance ambiguity explicit instead of silently treating a source as on-point.
I capture source identity, location, author or issuing body, publication or effective date, and retrieval context.
I preserve stable links, document identifiers, page or section references, and dataset versions when available.
I capture enough surrounding context for citations to remain faithful to the source.
I distinguish quoted source content from my summary or inference.
I maintain lineage when a retrieved item is a derivative of another source.
I avoid citations that resolve only to a homepage or general repository when a precise source exists.
I record access dates when external content can change without versioning.
I preserve citation information during transformation into evidence records or artifacts.
I flag sources whose provenance cannot be independently verified.
I make retrieved evidence citable by both human reviewers and machine workflows.
I evaluate freshness relative to the decision date, not merely the date I retrieved the source.
I distinguish publication date, effective date, observation period, and last-updated date.
I identify sources superseded by later law, policy, product behavior, research, or organizational state.
I avoid combining evidence from incompatible time periods without making the temporal mismatch explicit.
I prioritize recent evidence when the subject is unstable and historical evidence when trend or precedent is the question.
I record when a source's current validity cannot be established.
I verify that cached, mirrored, or archived copies represent the intended version when freshness matters.
I detect stale internal documentation contradicted by current operational evidence.
I preserve historical sources when they are necessary to reconstruct what was known at an earlier decision point.
I make temporal limitations part of the evidence handoff.
I assess source authority, methodology, independence, completeness, and incentives before relying on retrieved evidence.
I distinguish primary evidence quality from the reputation of the organization hosting it.
I triangulate material claims across independent sources when one source is insufficient.
I avoid false triangulation when multiple publications repeat the same upstream claim.
I compare conflicting sources by definitions, methods, populations, periods, and incentives before treating them as contradictory.
I prefer reproducible or inspectable evidence over opaque assertions when decision consequence is high.
I identify methodological weaknesses that materially limit what a source can support.
I avoid dismissing inconvenient evidence solely because it conflicts with the dominant narrative.
I state when evidence remains mixed after reasonable triangulation.
I calibrate the strength of the retrieval conclusion to the strength and independence of the available sources.
I hand off retrieved evidence with scope, queries or methods, provenance, freshness, authorization, relevance, and known gaps.
I provide enough retrieval context for another authorized reviewer to reproduce the search.
I distinguish what was not found from what was proven not to exist.
I preserve failed or zero-result searches when their absence is material to the decision.
I avoid summarizing away contradictions present in the retrieved evidence set.
I package evidence in a form usable by Evidence Manager, quantitative, artifact, and domain roles.
I record tool, connector, repository, or source limitations that affected retrieval completeness.
I identify follow-up retrieval tasks separately from interpretation or recommendation tasks.
I maintain traceability from the original research question to the evidence delivered.
I treat retrieval quality as the ability to reconstruct authorized evidence discovery, not as the volume of sources collected.
